questions.question: What does dotnet/runtime do, and who calls or runs it?
questions.answer: The repository builds .NET runtime engines, libraries and shared dotnet host/installers across platforms. Managed applications run on these engines and call library APIs; the host launches applications. System.Net.Http is only the selected library slice.

evidence.excerpt:
This repo contains the code to build the .NET runtime, libraries and shared host (`dotnet`) installers for
all supported platforms, as well as the sources to .NET runtime and libraries.

## What is .NET?

Official Starting Page: <https://dotnet.microsoft.com>

* [How to use .NET](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/get-started) (with VS, VS Code, command-line CLI)
  * [Install official releases](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download)
  * [Documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core) (Get Started, Tutorials, Porting from .NET Framework, API reference, ...)
    * [Deploying apps](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/deploying)

### Build Components

- **Runtime**: The execution engine for managed code. There are two different implementations, both written in C or C++:
  - *CoreCLR*: The comprehensive execution engine originally born from .NET Framework. Its source code lives under the [src/coreclr](/src/coreclr) subtree.
  - *Mono*: A slimmer runtime than CoreCLR, originally born open-source to bring .NET and C# support to non-Windows platforms. Due to its lightweight nature, it is less affected in terms of speed when working with the *Debug* configuration. Its source code lives under the [src/mono](/src/mono) subtree.

- **CoreLib** *(also known as System.Private.CoreLib)*: The lowest level managed library. It is directly related to the runtime, which means it must be built in the matching configuration (e.g. Building a *Debug* runtime means *CoreLib* must also be in *Debug*). The `clr` subset includes both, the *Runtime* and the *CoreLib* components, so you usually don't have to worry about that. There are, however, some special cases where you might need to build the components separately. The runtime agnostic code for this library can be found at [src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src](/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/README.md).

- **Libraries**: The bulk of dll's providing the rest of the functionality to the runtime. The libraries can be built in their own configuration, regardless of which one the runtime is using. Their source code lives under the [src/libraries](/src/libraries) subtree.

## Building the Repo

The main script that will be in charge of most of the building you might want to do is the `build.sh`, or `build.cmd` on Windows, located at the root of the repo. This script receives as arguments the subset(s) you might want to build, as well as multiple parameters to configure your build, such as the configuration, target operating system, target architecture, and so on.

The main subset values are:

- `Clr`: The full CoreCLR runtime, which consists of the runtime itself and the CoreLib components.
- `Libs`: All the libraries components, excluding their tests. This includes the libraries' native parts, refs, source assemblies, and their packages and test infrastructure.
- `Packs`: The shared framework packs, archives, bundles, installers, and the framework pack tests.
- `Host`: The .NET hosts, packages, hosting libraries, and their tests.
- `Mono`: The Mono runtime and its CoreLib.

questions.question: Name the principal repository components and responsibilities beyond HTTP.
questions.answer: CoreCLR and Mono are execution engines; System.Private.CoreLib is the lowest-level managed library; src/libraries holds wider APIs. Host supplies hosts and hosting libraries, Packs supplies framework packs/archives/installers. System.Net.Http is under libraries.

questions.question: Which languages, build systems and boundaries organize dotnet/runtime?
questions.answer: Engines use C/C++; managed libraries such as System.Net.Http use C# and SDK-style MSBuild csproj platform targets. CoreCLR has CMake. Root build.sh/build.cmd coordinate clr, mono, libs, host and packs subsets, not one HTTP package.

**NOTE:** If you plan on using Docker to work on the runtime repo, read [this doc](/docs/workflow/using-docker.md) first. It explains how to set up, as well as the images and containers to prepare you to follow the building and testing instructions in the next sections.

### General Overview

Running the script (`build.sh`/`build.cmd`) with no arguments will build the whole repo in *Debug* configuration, for the OS and architecture of your machine. A typical dev workflow only one or two components at a time, so it is more efficient to just build those. This is done by means of the `-subset` flag. For example, for CoreCLR, it would be:

```bash
./build.sh -subset clr
```

The main subset values are:

- `Clr`: The full CoreCLR runtime, which consists of the runtime itself and the CoreLib components.
- `Libs`: All the libraries components, excluding their tests. This includes the libraries' native parts, refs, source assemblies, and their packages and test infrastructure.
- `Packs`: The shared framework packs, archives, bundles, installers, and the framework pack tests.
- `Host`: The .NET hosts, packages, hosting libraries, and their tests.
- `Mono`: The Mono runtime and its CoreLib.

questions.question: Where does the selected public HTTP GET use begin on the sockets path?
questions.answer: Applications construct HttpClient, optionally injecting a handler. GetAsync overloads converge on SendAsync(CreateRequestMessage(HttpMethod.Get,...)); default construction chooses HttpClientHandler. The selected sockets path can differ from other platform/injected handler paths.
requiredFacts: GetAsync creates GET request then SendAsync

questions.question: Where is X, HTTP redirect method rewriting, implemented?
questions.answer: RedirectHandler.SendAsync and RequestRequiresForceGet implement it. POST becomes GET for 300/301/302; 303 rewrites all methods except GET/HEAD. Rewrite clears content and chunked encoding; the helper does not force GET for 307/308.

questions.question: Which internal components does A, SocketsHttpHandler.SetupHandlerChain, directly use?
questions.answer: It clones settings, creates HttpConnectionPoolManager and HttpConnectionHandler, conditionally wraps metrics, diagnostics and redirect handlers and invokes a decompression factory. Interlocked.CompareExchange publishes one chain. Constructors prove dependencies, but optional stages are configuration dependent.

questions.question: For R, sockets-based POST receiving an allowed 302 redirect, give the supported path and outcome.
questions.answer: HttpClient.SendAsync calls HttpMessageInvoker.SendAsync, dispatching to its handler. HttpClientHandler on the sockets path forwards to SocketsHttpHandler and its chain. RedirectHandler accepts Location, changes RequestUri and rewrites POST to GET without content, then resends via inner handler. Injected/platform dispatch and network response are runtime boundaries; wrappers depend on settings.
requiredFacts: Redirect URI and POST -> GET rewrite

questions.question: If Y, RedirectHandler construction/semantics, changes, which direct consumer is evidenced?
questions.answer: SocketsHttpHandler.SetupHandlerChain constructs RedirectHandler when _allowAutoRedirect is true, supplying redirect limit and credential-dependent disableAuthOnRedirect. This proves a consumer; user-visible effects depend on settings and server responses.

questions.question: Which tests exercise X, redirect method rewriting, and how do they enter implementation?
questions.answer: Common/tests/System/Net/Http/HttpClientHandlerTest.AutoRedirect.cs provides RedirectStatusCodesOldMethodsNewMethods and AllowAutoRedirect_True_ValidateNewMethodUsedOnRedirection. It creates client/handler, sends to a loopback redirect origin and asserts redirected method and final 200. Shared handler configuration selects the implementation; no execution is claimed.

questions.question: Where does Z, redirect Location, enter and get transformed?
questions.answer: GetUriForRedirect checks status then response.Headers.Location. Missing Location stops redirects; relative values resolve against request URI and omitted fragments inherit the original. Secure-to-insecure and unsupported schemes are blocked. SendAsync assigns accepted RequestUri before resending.
